newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian party takes tough royalist stance.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian party takes tough royalist stance.

text.p: Cambodia's royalist FUNCINPEC party of co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh wrapped up a three-day congress on Friday by adopting a platform likely to provoke more friction with its coalition partners.
FUNCINPEC, which is feuding with co-Premier Hun Sen's ex- communist Cambodian People's Pary (CPP) over the future of the monarchy, resolved to fight for the royalists' place in politics.
It also pushed for the return of two exiled princes.

Ranariddh said FUNCINPEC would ask his father King Norodom Sihanouk to grant amnesty to Norodom Sirivudh -- exiled for an alleged plot to kill Hun Sen -- and Norodom Chakrapong, a former CPP official exiled after a filed coup bid in 1994.
Sirivudh has indicated he will return in mid-April and Chakrapong has said he would also like to return to his homeland, raising the ire of Hun Sen.
FUNCINPEC adopted five other resolutions at the congress on Friday, including support for the monarchy.
Adding to the volatile mix, Ranariddh announced that a group of former Khmer Rouge guerrillas would join his political alliance.
Ranariddh and Hun Sen have been competing for the loyalty of thousands of defectors from the Khmer Rouge, whose 1975-79 rule left more than one million dead.
The prince reasserted plans to file a complaint against Hun Sen with the United Nations Commission on Human Rights in Geneva.

In the past week, Hun Sen has vowed to ask Sihanouk to ban royal family members from politics unless they renounced their royal status and warned he would cancel coming elections if the king abdicated to enter politics.
Analysts said the FUNCINPEC congress was a predictable reaction to Hun Sen's statements.
"They are the royalist party. If they don't stand up for that what do they stand for?" one analyst said.

The feud between Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who formed an uneasy coalition following U.N.-sponsored polls in 1993, irritates many international donors as well as some moderates in both parties, analysts said.
"People in the international community are going to lose patience," said the analyst.
While FUNCINPEC called for international observers at local and national elections scheduled in 1997 and 1998, not all donors would want to help because of the friction, observers said.
